city.name: Jerusalem
summary: Holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, Jerusalem had perhaps 20,000 to 30,000 people in 1099. The crusaders took it in July 1099 and ruled it until Saladin's conquest in October 1187, and again by treaty from 1229 to 1244.

Scrub the timeline to see the siege camps of 1099 and 1187, the Dome of the Rock become the Templum Domini, al-Aqsa become the Templars' headquarters, and the changes Saladin and his heirs made after 1187. Slide 'Then and Today' to compare with the Old City now.
city.note: Building outlines and the line of the walls are from OpenStreetMap. The walls drawn are the Ottoman walls, which follow the medieval line closely; the medieval walls also had a dry moat on the north. Siege camp positions follow the chronicles and are approximate. Quarter labels mark rough centres only.

properties.name: Mount of Olives
properties.description: The ridge east of the city, across the Kidron valley. On 8 July 1099 the crusaders walked barefoot in procession round the walls and up the Mount of Olives to hear sermons, while the defenders jeered from the walls.

properties.name: Mount Zion
properties.description: The hill south-west of the walled city, outside the walls in 1099. Christians honoured it as the site of the Last Supper and of Mary's death. Raymond of Toulouse attacked from here.

properties.name: City walls
description: The walls in 1099 were the Fatimid circuit, rebuilt after an earthquake in 1033. They left Mount Zion and the old City of David outside, and a dry moat guarded the north side.

Fearing the Fifth Crusade, the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, al-Muazzam Isa, had them pulled down in 1219, so Frederick II received an open city in 1229. The line drawn here is the Ottoman wall of 1537 to 1541, built largely on the medieval foundations.

properties.name: Walls pulled down in 1219
properties.description: Al-Muazzam Isa demolished the walls in 1219 so that crusaders could not hold the city if they took it. Many residents left. Jerusalem stayed unwalled until the Ottomans rebuilt the walls in the 1530s.

properties.name: David's Gate (Bab al-Khalil)
properties.description: Today's Jaffa Gate, beside the citadel. The road from the port of Jaffa and the pilgrims' road came in here.

properties.name: St Stephen's Gate (Bab al-Amud)
properties.description: Today's Damascus Gate, the main gate on the north side. Crusaders named it after the first Christian martyr, said to have been stoned outside.

properties.name: Gate of Flowers (Bab al-Sahira)
properties.description: Today's Herod's Gate. Near here, on 15 July 1099, Godfrey's men crossed from their siege tower onto the wall. Saladin's miners broke through close by in 1187.

properties.name: Gate of Jehoshaphat (Bab al-Asbat)
properties.description: Today's Lions' Gate, leading down to the Kidron valley and the Mount of Olives.

properties.name: Golden Gate (Bab al-Rahma)
properties.description: A walled-up gate into the Temple Mount. The crusaders opened it twice a year, on Palm Sunday and on the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross.

properties.name: Zion Gate (Bab al-Nabi Dawud)
properties.description: The south gate, facing Mount Zion. Raymond of Toulouse's men attacked this side in 1099.

properties.name: Haram al-Sharif (Temple Mount)
properties.description: The great platform built by Herod for the Jewish Temple, destroyed by the Romans in AD 70. Muslims call it the Noble Sanctuary, the place of Muhammad's Night Journey. When the crusaders broke in on 15 July 1099, many people fled here and were killed.

properties.name: Temple Mount (Templum Domini precinct)
properties.description: Under crusader rule the platform was Christian ground. Canons served the Templum Domini, and the Templars took over the south end round al-Aqsa.

properties.name: Haram al-Sharif (Temple Mount)
properties.description: Saladin restored the Haram to Islam in 1187. It stayed in Muslim hands even during Frederick II's treaty of 1229 to 1244, which gave the rest of the city to the Franks.

properties.name: Dome of the Rock
properties.description: Built in 691 by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik over the rock from which Muhammad is said to have risen to heaven, and which Jewish tradition places at the heart of the Temple.

properties.name: Templum Domini (Dome of the Rock)
description: The crusaders took the Dome of the Rock for the Temple of the Lord, where Christ was presented as a child. They put a gold cross on the dome, an altar on the rock, and appointed Augustinian canons to serve it.
Pilgrims chipped off pieces of the rock as relics, so the canons covered it with marble slabs and an iron grille, parts of which survive.

properties.name: Dome of the Rock
properties.description: When Saladin took the city in 1187 the great cross was pulled down from the dome, the marble removed from the rock and the building purified with rosewater.

properties.name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
properties.description: The congregational mosque at the south end of the Haram, rebuilt by the Fatimids after an earthquake. Crusader and Muslim writers both describe a massacre here in 1099.

properties.name: Royal palace (Temple of Solomon)
properties.description: The first crusader kings lived in al-Aqsa, which they called the Temple of Solomon. Around 1120 Baldwin II gave it to the new order of knights, who took their name from it: the Templars.

properties.name: Templars' headquarters (Temple of Solomon)
description: Headquarters of the Knights Templar. They added halls and a church, and used the vaults under the platform, known as Solomon's Stables, for their horses.

The Muslim nobleman Usama ibn Munqidh, visiting in peacetime, wrote that the Templars, his friends, let him pray in a small mosque beside it, and stopped a newly arrived Frank who tried to turn him to face east.

properties.name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
properties.description: Saladin restored al-Aqsa as a mosque and installed the carved wooden pulpit that Nur ad-Din had made in Aleppo years before, ready for the day Jerusalem was retaken. It stood there until an arson attack in 1969.

properties.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
description: Built over the places of Christ's crucifixion and tomb. The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim had it destroyed in 1009; the Byzantine emperor paid for its rebuilding in the 1040s. News of the destruction still echoed when the crusade was preached.

The crusaders rebuilt it as one great Romanesque church, consecrated on 15 July 1149, fifty years to the day after the city fell. Saladin left it open to Christian pilgrims in 1187, under Muslim keyholders.

properties.name: Tower of David (citadel)
properties.description: The citadel by the western gate. In 1099 the Fatimid governor Iftikhar al-Dawla held out here after the walls fell, then surrendered to Raymond of Toulouse and was allowed to leave with his guard. The crusader kings later made it their residence.

properties.name: Hospital of St John
properties.description: A hospice for pilgrims, founded by merchants from Amalfi before the crusade, grew into a great hospital that a pilgrim said could hold 2,000 patients. Its brothers became the Knights Hospitaller.

properties.name: Saladin's hospital (al-Bimaristan al-Salahi)
properties.description: After 1187 Saladin turned part of the Hospitallers' buildings into a Muslim hospital, endowed with rents for its upkeep.

properties.name: Church of St Anne
properties.description: A Romanesque church built around 1138 on the traditional site of the house of Mary's parents, beside a convent of Benedictine nuns.

properties.name: Salahiyya madrasa (St Anne's)
properties.description: In 1192 Saladin made St Anne's a school of Islamic law, the Salahiyya madrasa. The inscription over its door still names him. Because it was not pulled down, it is the best preserved crusader church in the city.

properties.name: Mosque of Omar
properties.description: Built in 1193 by Saladin's son al-Afdal opposite the Holy Sepulchre, on the spot where, by tradition, the caliph Umar prayed in 638 rather than inside the church, so that Muslims would not later claim it.

properties.name: Cathedral of St James (Armenian)
properties.description: The cathedral of the Armenian community, rebuilt in the 12th century. Armenians were close allies of the crusaders, and Armenian queens of Jerusalem were patrons.

properties.name: St Mary of Mount Zion (the Cenacle)
properties.description: A crusader church on Mount Zion, outside the walls, enclosing the room honoured as the place of the Last Supper. The upper room that survives is a Gothic hall of the crusader period.

properties.name: Ramban Synagogue
properties.description: In 1267 the Catalan rabbi Moses ben Nahman (Nahmanides) found Jerusalem with only two Jewish families and made a ruined house into a synagogue. It became the centre of a revived community.

properties.name: Jewish quarter
properties.description: Under the Fatimids the Jewish community lived in the north-east of the city. Many were killed in 1099; survivors were ransomed and Jews were barred from living in the city.

properties.name: Patriarch's quarter
properties.description: The Latin patriarch's quarter round the Holy Sepulchre, with his palace and the canons' houses.

properties.name: Syrian quarter (Juiverie)
properties.description: Around 1115 King Baldwin I repopulated the empty north-east, the old Jewish quarter, with Syrian Christians from across the Jordan. The Franks still called it the Juiverie, the Jewry.

properties.name: Armenian quarter
properties.description: The Armenian community round the Cathedral of St James, in the south-west corner of the city. It has stayed here ever since.

properties.name: German quarter
properties.description: Round the church and hospice of St Mary of the Germans, for German-speaking pilgrims.

properties.name: Maghrebi quarter
properties.description: Founded by Saladin's son al-Afdal for pilgrims and settlers from North Africa, beside the western wall of the Haram.

properties.name: Jewish quarter
properties.description: Saladin invited Jews back after 1187, and communities came from North Africa, France and England. In 1267 Nahmanides founded his synagogue here.

properties.name: Tancred
properties.description: Tancred camped by the north-west corner tower, later called Tancred's Tower.

properties.name: Robert of Normandy and Robert of Flanders
properties.description: The two Roberts camped on the north side, facing St Stephen's Gate.

properties.name: Godfrey's siege tower
properties.description: On the night of 9 to 10 July Godfrey had his siege tower taken apart and rebuilt further east, where the wall was weaker. On 15 July his men crossed from it onto the wall, and the city fell.

properties.name: Raymond of Toulouse
properties.description: Raymond camped first by David's Gate, then moved to Mount Zion. His tower was badly damaged by the defenders' fire. When the north wall fell, the Fatimid governor surrendered to him in the citadel.

properties.name: Saladin's first camp
properties.description: Saladin first attacked the west wall by David's Gate, but the sun was in his archers' eyes in the mornings.

properties.name: Saladin's camp and mines
properties.description: On 26 September Saladin moved his army to the north side. His miners brought down a stretch of wall near the Gate of Flowers, close to where the crusaders broke in in 1099. Balian of Ibelin then negotiated the surrender.
